claims.evidence: This is an observation from the LN01 simulation trajectories.

claims.claim: In both apo and MPER-TM-bound LN01 replicates, several POPC binding events were observed within the CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove at atomic accuracy when compared to dodecyl-PC headgroup position in LN01 X-ray structures.
claims.source: In both apo and MPER-TM-bound replicates, several POPC binding events were observed within the CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove at atomic accuracy when compared to dodecyl-PC headgroup position in LN01 X-ray structures, with the same sidechain interactions (Figure 3E–J).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and experimental structures.

claims.claim: Phospholipids in LN01's CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove site have much lower kinetic stability and occupancy (~30% and ~40% for MPER-TM-bound and apo, respectively) compared to other bnAbs.
claims.source: In contrast to PGZL1, 4E10, and 10E8 simulations, phospholipids in LN01's CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove site have much lower kinetic stability and occupancy: ~30% and~40% aggregate occupancy for MPER-TM-bound and apo, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of binding occupancy across different antibodies.

claims.claim: An additional new CDR-phospholipid binding site termed the Loading Site was observed reproducibly across apo and MPER-TM-bound LN01 trajectories at a groove comprised of CDR-H2, CDR-H3, and FR-L2.
claims.source: Two interesting behaviors stood out in LN01 simulations. First, an additional new CDR-phospholipid binding site was observed reproducibly across apo and MPER-TM-bound trajectories at an alternative groove comprised of and CDR-H2, CDR-H3, and FR-L2 we termed the Loading Site (Figure 3E–J).
claims.evidence: This is a novel finding from the LN01 simulations.

claims.claim: The Loading site in LN01 was occupied more often than the X-ray site: 78% and 58% simulation time for MPER-TM-bound and apo LN01 replicates respectively.
claims.source: The Loading site was occupied more often than the X-ray site: 78% and 58% simulation time for MPER-TM-bound and apo LN01 replicates respectively (Figure 3I, J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measure of binding occupancy from simulation data.

claims.claim: Antigen-free LN01 sampled a broader range of geometries at the membrane surface compared to MPER-TM-bound LN01.
claims.source: The second notable behavior observed was that antigen-free LN01 sampled a broader range of geometries at the membrane surface, characterized by two angles describing the Fab relative to the membrane (Figure 3A–D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing apo and antigen-bound simulation ensembles.

claims.claim: LN01 complexed with MPER-TM was more deeply and extensively embedded than LN01 alone and resulted in a more focused conformation landscape.
claims.source: LN01 complexed with MPER-TM was more deeply and extensively embedded than LN01 alone and resulted in a more focused conformation landscape – aligned with the minimal dynamics of the MPER-TM orientation.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of conformational ensembles between apo and antigen-bound states.

claims.claim: Apo LN01 heavily samples the major conformation adopted in MPER-TM-bound state, suggesting LN01's surface-bound geometry is predisposed for transmembrane antigen engagement.
claims.source: Critically, while apo LN01 favors a different geometry (positive Rotation angle) its membrane surface ensemble heavily samples the major conformation adopted in MPER-TM-bound state (negative Rotation angle; Figure 3B, D). This observation that LN01's surface-bound geometry is predisposed for transmembrane antigen engagement suggests that maturing bnAbs' sequences and structures are primed for the membrane interaction key to access MPER and form the neuralization complex.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from simulation data with an interpretation about antibody maturation.

claims.claim: Fab's simulated in CG representation with elastic network restraints maintained the protein fold (<2 Å backbone RMSD) and retained key heavy-light inter-domain contacts.
claims.source: Fab's simulated in CG representation with elastic network restraints maintained the protein fold (<2 Å backbone RMSD) and retained key heavy-light inter-domain contacts, informing that this polar bead model rigidly presents the Fab macroscopic surface features critical for mediating bilayer surface interactions, that is hydrophobic patches, charge, polarity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This validates the CG model by showing it maintains structural integrity.

claims.claim: In 18 replicate spontaneous insertion CG simulations for each of 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, CDR-directed association stable within the lipid bilayer (>1 µs) was observed within 10, 14, and 12 trajectories, respectively.
claims.source: In 18 replicate simulations for each of 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, we observed CDR-directed association stable within the lipid bilayer (>1 µs) within 10, 14, and 12 trajectories, respectively (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative summary of CG simulation results.

claims.claim: Bovine serum albumin (BSA) showed drastically reduced membrane contact events (2/18) and lack of sustained insertion in CG simulations.
claims.source: As a reference, bovine serum albumin (BSA) was tested similarly. BSA's documented weak affinity for lipid bilayer association (low millimolar; Ruggeri et al., 2013) aligns with the drastically reduced membrane contact events (2/18) and lack of sustained insertion observed (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a negative control result from CG simulations.

claims.claim: Non-neutralizing anti-gp41 antibody 13h11 exhibited negligible insertion and only sparse 'scanning' events in CG simulations.
claims.source: Non-neutralizing anti-gp41 antibody 13h11 having no detectable lipid bilayer interaction by bilayer interferometry (Alam et al., 2009; Nicely et al., 2010) also exhibited negligible insertion and only sparse 'scanning' events, starkly contrasting the bnAbs' behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a negative control result from CG simulations consistent with experimental data.

claims.claim: CG simulations readily distinguish MPER bnAbs with high propensity for lipid interaction (low micromolar affinity) from non-specific and low affinity lipid interactions.
claims.source: Thus, these CG simulations readily distinguish MPER bnAbs with high propensity for lipid interaction (low micromolar affinity) from non-specific and low affinity lipid interactions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing bnAb CG simulations with BSA and 13h11 controls.

claims.claim: Fab conformational ensembles and protein-lipid interaction patterns from both CG approaches heavily overlapped with the primary geometry observed for each respective bnAb all-atom trajectories.
claims.source: Fab conformational ensembles and protein-lipid interaction patterns from both CG approaches heavily overlapped with the primary geometry observed for each respective bnAb all-atom trajectories, showing consistency between the two simulation models (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency between CG and all-atom simulation results.

claims.claim: CG 4E10 insertions across both methods adopted single conformations which were similar and all-atom-like.
claims.source: CG 4E10 insertions across both methods adopted single conformations which were similar and all-atom-like.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing CG and all-atom simulation results for 4E10.

claims.claim: PGZL1 and 10E8 showed more promiscuity by sampling alternative ab initio membrane-inserted geometries alongside their respective all-atom-like conformations in CG simulations.
claims.source: PGZL1 and 10E8 showed more promiscuity by sampling alternative ab initio membrane-inserted geometries alongside their respective all-atom-like conformations, with these states appearing consistently in both CG approaches but at different frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing CG simulation results for PGZL1 and 10E8.

claims.claim: For each bnAb, all sustained CG insertion events are CDR-directed.
claims.source: Overall, these CG simulations facilitate study of ab initio membrane insertion for MPER bnAbs, wherein we find all sustained events are CDR-directed, ruling out contributions from other Fab surface features.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion from analyzing all CG simulation trajectories.

claims.claim: For each of 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, three representative medoid Fab poses were extracted by clustering CG simulation frames and converted to all-atom detail to initiate unbiased MD simulation.
claims.source: For each of 4E10, PGZl1, and 10E8, three representative medoid Fab poses were extracted by clustering CG simulation frames (clusters A, B, C), and converting to all-atom detail to initiate unbiased MD simulation (Figure 6A, B).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for integrating CG and all-atom simulations.

claims.claim: For 4E10, trajectories initiated from all three CG-derived geometries drifted back to conformations very similar to those of initial pre-inserted all-atom trajectories and bound phospholipids at the CDR-H1 site.
claims.source: For 4E10, trajectories initiated from all three geometries drifted back to conformations very similar to those of our initial pre-inserted all-atom trajectories and bound phospholipids at the CDR-H1 site (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: This shows that CG-derived conformations converge to biologically relevant states in all-atom simulations.

claims.claim: The 4E10 trajectory back-mapped from CG cluster A adopted deeper insertion and higher CDR-H1 phospholipid binding occupancy (>60%) compared to clusters B and C.
claims.source: Interestingly, the trajectory back-mapped from cluster A adopted deeper insertion and higher CDR-H1 phospholipid binding occupancy (>60%) compared to ensembles of clusters B and C trajectories, which were slightly tilted (rotation angle >0°) and less extensively inserted, indicating the latter geometries are likely less ideal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of different starting conformations and their outcomes.

claims.claim: For PGZL1, all-atom trajectories starting from CG clusters B and C converge to CDR-H-inserted conformations analogous to previous all-atom MD, and stably bind phospholipid headgroups at CDR-H1 (>50% occupancy).
claims.source: For PGZL1, all-atom trajectories starting from CG clusters B and C similarly converge to CDR-H-inserted conformations analogous to our previous all-atom MD, and stably bind phospholipid headgroups at CDR-H1 (>50% occupancy; Figure 6C–E).
claims.evidence: This shows successful integration of CG and all-atom simulations for PGZL1.

claims.claim: For 10E8, the all-atom trajectory from CG Cluster C started and finished in membrane-bound orientations analogous to the pre-inserted simulations and the bivalent CDR-L1 phospholipid complex readily formed with high occupancy (>70%).
claims.source: For 10E8, Cluster C started and finished in membrane-bound orientations analogous to the pre-inserted simulations (Figure 6C), although the Fab adopted a slightly different protein-lipid interaction pattern with much shallower CDR-H3 insertion, the bivalent CDR-L1 phospholipid complex still readily formed with high occupancy (>70%) (Figure 6D, E).
claims.evidence: This shows successful integration of CG and all-atom simulations for 10E8.

claims.claim: The all-atom simulation from one alternate 10E8 CG conformation (cluster A) rapidly dissociated from the membrane within 50 ns, showing this integrative MD distinguishes this state as an unstable likely artifact.
claims.source: All-atom simulation from one alternate conformation of 10E8, CG cluster A, rapidly dissociated from the membrane within 50 ns (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), showing this integrative MD distinguishes this state as an unstable likely artifact.
claims.evidence: This demonstrates that the integrative approach can identify unstable/artifactual conformations.

claims.claim: With one membrane-bound Fab, it is very unlikely a second Fab can simultaneously engage the bilayer due to restriction from the IgG hinge.
claims.source: The resulting full-length IgG geometries shows that with one membrane-bound Fab, it is very unlikely a second Fabs can simultaneously engage the bilayer due to restriction from the IgG hinge – except for the case of an extraordinarily flexible hinge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from modeling full-length IgG based on Fab orientations.

claims.source: Finally, we applied biased constant velocity atomistic simulations to compute the force required to dissociate a Fab bound to lipid bilayers – providing a binding strength estimate akin to force spectroscopy (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for estimating membrane binding strength.

claims.source: WAWA has similar Kd to MPER as 4E10, but significantly reduced affinity to empty HIV-like liposomes and neutralization efficacy (>100-fold higher IC50; Scherer et al., 2010; Kwon et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is experimental data from cited studies.

claims.claim: Across replicates from different starting states for 4E10 (n=9) and WAWA (n=11), rupture force calculations showed average forces of 63.8±2.8 kJ/nm/mol and 48.0±2.6 kJ/nm/mol, respectively.
claims.source: Across replicates from different starting states for 4E10 (n=9) and WAWA (n=11), rupture force calculations showed average forces (± S.E.M.) of 63.8±2.8 kJ/nm/mol and 48.0±2.6 kJ/nm/mol, respectively (Figure 7D, E), correctly indicating the 4E10 ensemble has a stronger membrane interaction (32 ± 13%; p-value <0.001).
claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from pulling simulations showing statistically significant differences.

claims.claim: Mature PGZL1 has relatively high affinity to the MPER epitope peptide (Kd = 10 nM) and demonstrates great breadth and potency, neutralizing 84% of a 130-strain panel.
claims.source: Mature PGZL1 has relatively high affinity to the MPER epitope peptide (Kd = 10 nM) and demonstrates great breadth and potency, neutralizing 84% of a 130-strain panel.

claims.source: An 'Intermediate' PGZL1 with V-gene germline reversion (gVmDmJ, 100% CDR-H3 identity) showed a modest affinity loss (Kd = 64 nM), while neutralization potency and breadth (12%) were more substantially reduced than expected due to affinity alone – attributed to impaired lipid bilayer interactions (Zhang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study.

claims.source: The fully 'Germline' reverted variant (gVgDgM) had no detectable MPER peptide affinity or neutralization.

claims.claim: Significantly lower pulling forces were required to dissociate Intermediate and Germline PGZL1 from bilayers (37.5±14.9 and 41.2±11.7 kJ/nm/mol respectively) than for mature PGZL1 (56.1±11.6 kJ/nm/mol; p<0.003).
claims.source: Significantly lower pulling forces were required to dissociate Intermediate and Germline PGZL1 from bilayers, 37.5±14.9 kJ/nm/mol and 41.2±11.7 kJ/nm/mol respectively, than for mature PGZL1, 56.1±11.6 kJ/nm/mol (p<0.003; Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from pulling simulations showing statistically significant differences.

claims.source: While the difference in Germline and Intermediate force distributions was not significant (p>0.4), more higher force events were observed for the Intermediate.

claims.claim: bnAb phospholipid binding features are acquired and honed along the maturation pathway, connecting positive selection of antibody-lipid interactions with neutralization efficacy.
claims.source: These results provide further evidence that bnAb phospholipid binding features are acquired and honed along the maturation pathway, entrenching the connection between positive selection of antibody-lipid interactions and neutralization efficacy.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PGZL1 variant pulling simulation results.

claims.source: Initial membrane-bound Fab conformations were computed using PPM2.03735 (Lomize et al., 2012), globally optimizing protein insertion based on per-residue hydrophobicity and solvation, each resulting in reasonable predictions with CDR-H3 embedded.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational method used to generate initial structures.

claims.source: The coordinates for Fab models were obtained from X-ray crystallography structures for each antibody (PDB id: 2FX9, 6O3D, 5T85 for 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8 respectively).
claims.evidence: This describes the source of structural models used in the study.

claims.source: Atomistic simulations were performed with Gromacs 2021 and CHARMM36 forcefield.
claims.evidence: This describes the simulation software and parameters used.

claims.source: A 2 fs time step was used along with the LINCS constraint algorithm during the equilibration stage.
claims.evidence: This describes the simulation parameters used.

claims.source: Coarse grain representations of Fab models were generated based on the Martini version 2.2 four to one mapping of heavy atoms to bead representation using the martinize script with an elastic network that defined harmonic bonds at default parameters.
claims.evidence: This describes the coarse-graining methodology used.

results.result: All-atom MD simulations accurately predict ab initio phospholipid binding at CDR-H1 sites for 4E10 and PGZL1 with sub-Ångström accuracy compared to X-ray structures. The simulations show rapid binding (within 20 ns), high stability (>80% occupancy), and low mobility (<1 Å RMSF) of phospholipid complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19, C27, C29, C30, C31 provide quantitative validation showing 0.6-0.7 Å RMSD to experimental structures, rapid binding kinetics, and high occupancy (>80%). Claims C32-C33 detail the molecular interactions and structural stability. The convergence between simulation and experiment across multiple replicates strongly supports this result.

results.result: All-atom MD simulations of 10E8 reveal a bivalent phosphocholine binding site involving both CDR-L1 (choline moiety) and FR-L3 (phosphate moiety), with >70% occupancy and high stability. This differs slightly from previous crystallographic interpretations but is consistent with experimental mutagenesis data.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 provide detailed structural and quantitative data showing consistent binding across all four replicates with high occupancy and sub-Ångström stability. Claim C43 provides experimental validation through mutagenesis showing >500-fold reduction in neutralization with minimal impact on MPER affinity, supporting the functional importance of this site.

results.result: Framework region 3 of the heavy chain (FR-H3) extensively intercalates into the bilayer surface for both 4E10 and PGZL1, demonstrating that germline-encoded antibody features contribute significantly to membrane binding mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 consistently identify FR-H3 membrane intercalation across simulations of both antibodies. The observation is novel and reproducible, with molecular details provided about the types of interactions (charged residues mediating headgroup contacts). This finding has clear implications for vaccine design as stated in C36.

results.result: Structural bioinformatics analysis reveals that the CDR-H1 phosphate binding motif in 4E10/PGZL1 is relatively prevalent in protein structures but rare as a phosphate-binding motif (4 cases), while 10E8's FR-L3 site is a common phosphate-binding motif (23 cases).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 provide quantitative results from database searches showing 10^5-10^6 geometrically similar loops but only 4 phosphate-binding cases for CDR-H1 and 23 for FR-L3. This orthogonal validation supports the biological relevance of the simulation-predicted binding sites, particularly for the novel FR-L3 site in 10E8.

results.result: LN01 simulations reveal two phospholipid binding sites: the crystallographic CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove site (30-40% occupancy) and a novel 'Loading Site' at CDR-H2-H3-FR-L2 (58-78% occupancy). Apo LN01 samples conformations predisposed for MPER-TM engagement.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 provide quantitative occupancy data for both sites across multiple replicates, with the Loading Site showing higher occupancy than the crystallographic site. Claims C61-C63 demonstrate that apo LN01 samples the MPER-TM-bound conformation, supporting a pre-organization mechanism. The consistency across replicates and comparison with experimental structures supports this result.

results.result: Coarse-grained simulations with elastic network restraints successfully capture spontaneous membrane insertion of MPER bnAbs (10-14 of 18 trajectories showing stable insertion) while distinguishing them from negative controls (BSA: 2/18, 13h11: negligible). CG conformations overlap with all-atom simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 provide quantitative validation of the CG approach through structural stability metrics, insertion frequencies, and negative controls. Claims C69-C72 demonstrate consistency between CG and all-atom methods. The inclusion of appropriate negative controls (BSA, 13h11) with known experimental properties strengthens the validation.

results.result: Integration of CG and all-atom simulations through backmapping demonstrates that CG-derived membrane-bound conformations converge to biologically relevant states that form key phospholipid complexes. For 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, specific CG clusters successfully transition to stable all-atom conformations with high phospholipid binding occupancy (>50-70%).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 show successful convergence for multiple clusters across three antibodies with quantitative occupancy data. Claim C78 demonstrates that the method can identify unstable/artifactual conformations (10E8 cluster A dissociating within 50 ns), showing the approach has discriminatory power. This multi-scale integration is well-validated.

results.result: Constant velocity pulling simulations distinguish membrane binding strength between 4E10 (63.8±2.8 kJ/nm/mol) and its WAWA variant (48.0±2.6 kJ/nm/mol), correctly recapitulating the experimentally observed difference in membrane affinity and neutralization potency.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 provides statistically significant differences (p<0.001, 32±13% difference) that align with experimental observations in C81 showing >100-fold reduced neutralization for WAWA. The pulling simulation method successfully distinguishes variants with known differential membrane affinity, validating the computational approach.

results.result: Pulling simulations of PGZL1 maturation variants show that membrane binding affinity correlates with neutralization potency. Mature PGZL1 requires significantly higher forces for dissociation (56.1±11.6 kJ/nm/mol) than Intermediate (37.5±14.9) or Germline (41.2±11.7) variants (p<0.003), paralleling their neutralization breadth (84%, 12%, 0% respectively).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 provide experimental characterization and simulation data showing correlation between computational membrane affinity estimates and experimental neutralization potency. The statistically significant differences (C86, p<0.003) between mature and less mature variants support the conclusion in C88 that phospholipid binding features are acquired during maturation. However, the lack of significance between Germline and Intermediate (C87) suggests some limitations in resolution.

results.result: Background and context establishing that MPER-targeting bnAbs use membrane-lipid interactions as part of their neutralization mechanism, supported by prior experimental and structural studies.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C18) establish the scientific context through citations to prior work. They are well-supported by the cited literature and provide the rationale for the computational studies. Claims C13-C14 provide specific experimental evidence linking membrane binding to neutralization potency.

results.result: Methodological details for simulation setup including membrane composition, antibody structures, simulation parameters, and software used.
results.evaluation: These claims (C20-C26, C89-C93) describe the computational methodology. They are factual statements about simulation setup, parameters, and starting structures. The methods are clearly described and use standard, validated approaches (CHARMM36, Gromacs, Martini CG model).

results.result: One PGZL1 simulation captured a lipid exchange event where a POPC molecule bound for ~500 ns was replaced by a POPA molecule.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 describes a specific observation from one trajectory with supporting video evidence. While this is a single observation, it demonstrates the dynamic nature of lipid binding and is consistent with the overall picture of stable but exchangeable lipid complexes.

results.result: 4E10's CDR-H loops are more deeply buried and extensively contact lipid tails compared to PGZL1, which may explain 4E10's higher poly-specificity.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 makes an observation about differential membrane insertion depth between 4E10 and PGZL1 from simulation data, but the causal link to poly-specificity is speculative. While the observation is supported by simulation data, the mechanistic explanation for poly-specificity requires additional validation beyond what is presented.

results.result: Simulated membrane-bound Fab orientations are similar to those in cryo-EM structures of bnAb-bound Env, with the main difference being slightly more upright orientations in simulations (~15° difference). Conformational clustering reveals antibody-specific differences in phospholipid binding occupancy across substates.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide quantitative comparison with experimental structures showing good agreement with minor differences. Claims C51-C52 provide detailed conformational analysis showing antibody-specific behavior. The comparison with experimental structures validates the simulation approach.

results.result: Modeling of full-length IgG suggests that bivalent Fab-membrane engagement is unlikely due to hinge restrictions.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is based on structural modeling rather than simulation data. While the geometric argument is reasonable, it lacks the dynamic sampling and energetic considerations that would be needed to definitively rule out bivalent binding. The conclusion is plausible but requires experimental validation or more rigorous computational analysis.

results.result: All-atom MD simulations of 4E10 and PGZL1 predict ab initio phospholipid binding at CDR-H1 sites with atomic accuracy matching X-ray crystallography structures (0.6-0.7 Å RMSD). These phospholipid complexes form rapidly (within 20 ns), are highly stable (>80% occupancy, <1 Å RMSF), and involve specific hydrogen bonding networks that anchor the antibodies to membrane surfaces.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, stating the simulations 'accurately and reproducibly predict ab initio binding of phospholipids stably bound at specific CDR binding sites previously identified in co-crystal structures.' One reviewer notes the simulations 'recapitulate in several cases the binding sites of lipid head groups that were observed experimentally by X-ray crystallography' and that 'the simulated lipid phosphates bound within CDR-H1 have exceptional overlap with electron densities from respective lipid-soaked co-crystal structures.'

results.result: Framework region 3 of the heavy chain (FR-H3) extensively intercalates into the bilayer surface for both 4E10 and PGZL1, demonstrating that predominantly germline-encoded antibody surface features can provide significant contributions to membrane binding mechanism and surface orientation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this as a novel discovery, with one stating the authors 'discovered that a previously unappreciated framework region between loops 2-3 in the 4E10/PGZL1 heavy chain contributes to membrane association.' This finding is treated as an important mechanistic insight without critique.

results.result: 10E8 simulations reveal a bivalent phosphocholine binding site at the CDR-L1/FR-L3 groove with >70% occupancy. The phosphate moiety localizes to FR-L3 (offset 2.7 Å from the crystallographic CDR-L1 site), while the choline moiety occupies the precise crystallographic CDR-L1 site, coordinated by four unpaired backbone carbonyls.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that '10E8 simulations revealed several differences from published X-ray structures. Namely, a phosphatidylcholine binding site was offset and includes significant interaction with a nearby framework region.' The revised manuscript is noted to demonstrate 'these lipid interactions are robust to alterations in membrane composition and rigidity,' indicating reviewer acceptance of these findings.

results.result: LN01 simulations with and without MPER-TM antigen reveal two phospholipid binding sites: the crystallographic X-ray site (CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove, ~30-40% occupancy) and a novel 'Loading Site' (CDR-H2/CDR-H3/FR-L2 groove, 58-78% occupancy). Antigen-free LN01 samples broader membrane geometries but heavily samples the MPER-TM-bound conformation, suggesting the antibody is predisposed for transmembrane antigen engagement.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings, noting the simulations 'recapitulate lipid binding interactions solved in published crystallographic studies but also lead to the discovery of a novel lipid binding site the authors term the "Loading Site", which could guide future experiments with this antibody.' The observation about conformational predisposition is accepted without critique.

results.result: Structural bioinformatics analysis shows that the CDR-H1 loop backbone conformations of 4E10/PGZL1 are relatively prevalent in the protein universe (10^5 to 2×10^6 matches), but only 4 cases bind phosphate-type ligands, making this a rare protein-phospho-ligand motif. For 10E8, the FR-L3 beta-turn site is a hotspot for phosphate-type ligands (23 natural protein cases), while CDR-L1 shows only 1 case.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this analysis, stating 'these binding sites were further validated using a structural bioinformatics approach.' The combination of MD simulations and structural bioinformatics is described as 'a comprehensive approach to validate the identified binding sites,' indicating acceptance of these findings.

results.result: Coarse-grained (CG) simulations capture spontaneous CDR-directed membrane insertion for 4E10 (10/18 trajectories), PGZL1 (14/18), and 10E8 (12/18), while negative controls BSA (2/18) and non-neutralizing antibody 13h11 show drastically reduced insertion. CG results overlap with all-atom trajectories, demonstrating the approach distinguishes high-affinity lipid interactions from non-specific binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings, noting 'these CG simulations, which cannot resolve atomistic interactions, are nonetheless compelling because negative controls (ab 13h11, BSA) that should not associate with membrane indeed sample significantly less membrane.' The editor states the work 'provides insights into how broadly neutralizing antibodies associate with lipids,' indicating acceptance of the CG methodology and results.

results.result: Integration of CG and all-atom simulations shows that CG-derived membrane-bound geometries converge to biologically relevant conformations in all-atom MD. For 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, specific CG clusters produce stable all-atom trajectories with high phospholipid binding occupancy (>50-70%), while unstable CG conformations (e.g., 10E8 cluster A) rapidly dissociate, demonstrating the approach can distinguish functional from artifactual states.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this integrative approach, stating 'distinct geometries derived from CG simulations were then used to initialize all-atom MD simulations to study insertion in finer detail (e.g., phospholipid association), which largely recapitulate their earlier results, albeit with more unbiased sampling. The multiscale model of an initial CG study with broad geometric sampling, followed by all-atom MD, provides a generalized framework for such simulations.'

results.result: Steered MD pulling simulations correctly predict that 4E10 has stronger membrane binding than the WAWA variant (63.8±2.8 vs 48.0±2.6 kJ/nm/mol; 32±13% difference; p<0.001), consistent with experimental data showing WAWA has reduced lipid affinity and >100-fold reduced neutralization despite similar MPER affinity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this validation, stating the authors 'demonstrate that their model reliably predicts lower association energetics for known mutations in 4E10 that disrupt lipid binding.' This is treated as evidence that the computational approach can distinguish functional differences in membrane binding.

results.result: Pulling simulations along the PGZL1 maturation pathway show mature PGZL1 has significantly stronger membrane binding (56.1±11.6 kJ/nm/mol) than Intermediate (37.5±14.9) and Germline (41.2±11.7) variants (p<0.003), correlating with neutralization potency. This demonstrates that phospholipid binding features are acquired and honed during antibody maturation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the approach works for large differences but note limitations: 'the model does have limitations: namely, its ability to predict more subtle changes along a lineage-intermediate mutations that reduce lipid binding are indistinguishable from mutations that completely ablate lipid association.' The lack of significant difference between Intermediate and Germline (p>0.4) despite different neutralization profiles supports this critique. The editor notes 'a quantitative assessment of the underlying energetics remain difficult to obtain.'

results.result: The computational methodology employs Gromacs 2021 with CHARMM36 forcefield for all-atom simulations and Martini 2.2 coarse-graining with elastic network restraints. CG simulations maintain protein fold (<2 Å backbone RMSD) and effectively capture antibody membrane embedding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the methodological rigor, stating 'the MD simulations conducted throughout are rigorous and the analysis are extensive, creative, and biologically inspired.' One reviewer notes 'the use of multiscale MD simulations allows for a detailed exploration of the system at different time and length scales,' though cautions that 'coarse-grained simulations exhibit artifacts and thus require careful analysis.'

results.result: MPER-targeting bnAbs (4E10, PGZL1, 10E8, LN01) from unique lineages show varying lipid affinity that correlates with neutralization potency. Experimental evidence shows mutations enhancing lipid binding boost neutralization, while mutations reducing hydrophobicity drastically reduce neutralization despite minimal impact on antigen affinity. This supports a two-step neutralization mechanism where bnAbs first associate with membranes via CDR embedding, then laterally diffuse to engage Env at MPER.
results.evaluation: These are established findings from prior experimental work that reviewers accept as the foundation for the study. One reviewer states 'previous experimental studies demonstrated that membrane association drives avidity for several potent broadly HIV-neutralizing antibodies and its loss dramatically reduces neutralization.' The reviewers treat these as validated background knowledge supporting the computational investigation.

results.result: Compared to PGZL1, 4E10's CDR-H loops are more deeply buried and extensively contact lipid aliphatic tails, which may explain 4E10's higher poly-specificity.
results.evaluation: This observation from simulations is accepted by reviewers without critique. One reviewer notes the manuscript demonstrates 'lipid interactions are robust to alterations in membrane composition,' implicitly accepting the differential binding depth observations. The speculative interpretation about poly-specificity is presented cautiously ('may explain') and not challenged.

results.result: Simulated antigen-free Fabs favor similar membrane orientations as in experimental bnAb-bound Env structures, with the primary difference being that Env-bound Fabs adopt slightly more shallow approach angles (~15°). Conformational clustering reveals antibody-specific variance in phospholipid binding across substates, with 4E10 maintaining high CDR-H1 occupancy (86-98%) across all substates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these comparisons with experimental structures as validation of the simulation approach. The consistency between simulated and experimental orientations is treated as evidence supporting the computational methodology, with no critiques raised about these specific findings.

results.result: Modeling full-length IgG geometries based on Fab orientations suggests that with one membrane-bound Fab, it is very unlikely a second Fab can simultaneously engage the bilayer due to restriction from the IgG hinge, except for extraordinarily flexible hinges.
results.evaluation: This inference from modeling is accepted without critique by reviewers. It is presented as a logical consequence of the Fab orientation data and is consistent with the monovalent binding model implied by the experimental and simulation data.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations strongly support the findings about phospholipid binding at CDR sites (C3, C19, C27-C33). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative validation (0.6-0.7 Å RMSD, >80% occupancy), while peer reviewers highlight that simulations 'accurately and reproducibly predict ab initio binding' and 'recapitulate binding sites observed experimentally by X-ray crystallography.' Both mark as SUPPORTED with high confidence.

Perfect agreement on 10E8 findings (C39-C43). Both evaluations support the novel phosphatidylcholine binding site offset from published structures and FR-L3 involvement. OpenEval provides quantitative details (sub-Ångström stability, >500-fold reduction in neutralization), while peer reviewers note the findings are 'robust to alterations in membrane composition and rigidity.' Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Perfect agreement on FR-H3 membrane intercalation discovery (C35-C37). Both evaluations recognize this as a novel finding with implications for vaccine design. Peer reviewers describe it as 'a previously unappreciated framework region' contributing to membrane association, treating it as an important mechanistic insight. Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluations support the structural bioinformatics validation (C45-C48). OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative database search results (10^5-10^6 geometrically similar loops, only 4 and 23 phosphate-binding cases), while peer reviewers describe it as 'a comprehensive approach to validate the identified binding sites.' Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluations support LN01 findings (C57-C63), including the novel 'Loading Site' discovery. OpenEval provides quantitative occupancy data and emphasizes pre-organization mechanism, while peer reviewers note the discovery 'could guide future experiments with this antibody' and accept the conformational predisposition observations. Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Perfect agreement on CG methodology validation (C64-C72). Both evaluations emphasize the importance of negative controls (BSA, 13h11) and consistency between CG and all-atom methods. Peer reviewers note CG simulations are 'compelling because negative controls that should not associate with membrane indeed sample significantly less membrane.' Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Perfect agreement on multiscale integration approach (C73-C78). Both evaluations strongly support the CG-to-all-atom workflow. Peer reviewers explicitly state it 'provides a generalized framework for such simulations,' and OpenEval emphasizes the discriminatory power (identifying unstable conformations). Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Perfect agreement on pulling simulation validation (C80-C82). Both evaluations support the method's ability to distinguish WAWA variant with reduced membrane affinity. OpenEval emphasizes statistical significance (p<0.001, 32±13% difference), while peer reviewers note the model 'reliably predicts lower association energetics for known mutations.' Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Significant disagreement on maturation analysis (C83-C88). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED despite noting lack of significance between Germline and Intermediate (C87), while peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting 'the model does have limitations: namely, its ability to predict more subtle changes along a lineage.' Peer reviewers emphasize that intermediate mutations are 'indistinguishable from mutations that completely ablate lipid association.'

Perfect agreement on background/context claims (C1-C2, C8-C18). Both evaluations support these as well-established findings from prior experimental work. OpenEval notes they are 'well-supported by the cited literature,' while peer reviewers accept them as 'validated background knowledge supporting the computational investigation.' Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluations support the computational methodology (C20-C26, C89-C93). OpenEval describes them as 'factual statements about simulation setup using standard, validated approaches,' while peer reviewers affirm 'the MD simulations conducted throughout are rigorous and the analysis are extensive, creative, and biologically inspired.' Both mark as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval evaluates C34 (lipid exchange observation from single trajectory) as SUPPORTED, noting it demonstrates dynamic nature of lipid binding. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.

Disagreement on differential insertion depth claim (C38). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting the causal link to poly-specificity is speculative and requires additional validation. Peer reviewers mark as SUPPORTED, accepting the observation without critique and noting the speculative interpretation is presented cautiously. Different standards for mechanistic speculation.

Perfect agreement on MPER-TM orientation comparisons (C49-C52). Both evaluations support the quantitative comparison with experimental structures and conformational analysis. Peer reviewers treat consistency with experimental structures as validation of simulation approach. Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Disagreement on bivalent binding inference (C79). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting it is based on structural modeling rather than simulation data and 'lacks the dynamic sampling and energetic considerations' needed for definitive conclusions. Peer reviewers mark as SUPPORTED, accepting it as a logical consequence of Fab orientation data without critique. Different standards for modeling-based inferences.
